item.title: Generative AI as a cognitive partner: personalised GPTs and differentiated learning in undergraduate teacher education
item.description:
Educational Technology Research and Development
Abstract Generative artificial intelligence is increasingly framed as a catalyst for deeper learning rather than simple automation. This design-based study investigated how personalised GPT agents were used as cognitive partners by pre-service teachers in an undergraduate Initial Teacher Education course in Digital Technologies within a Bachelor of Education (Secondary) programme. Drawing on distributed cognition, constructivism, cognitive load theory, and critical AI literacy, the intervention embedded personalised GPT agents within a university Canvas Learning Management System. Fourteen students configured and used agents aligned to curriculum goals, teaching contexts, pedagogical preferences, and weekly Prompt–Reflect–Refine tasks. Data included approximately 7,000 AI interactions, reflective journals, assessed lesson and assessment artefacts, and tutorial-group discussions. A hybrid inductive–deductive thematic analysis identified four recurrent functions in students’ use of the agents: conceptual tutor, co-designer, reflective mirror, and cognitive challenger. Across data sources, students reported clearer conceptual support, iterative planning, and reflective prompting, alongside risks of over-reliance, factual drift, and culturally narrow exemplars. The study contributes a context-specific model for LMS-integrated generative AI that foregrounds partnership, personalisation, judgement, and ethical reflexivity. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because the study was small-scale, single-site, and partly reliant on self-reported reflection.

item.title: AI Ingratiation in Content Generation: A Dual-Pathway Model of Intimacy and Authenticity
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in content generation, understanding how its interaction styles shape user responses is critical. This study examines AI ingratiation—AI-generated expressions of praise and flattery—and its effects on user perceptions and behavioral outcomes. A 2×2 online experiment reveals that AI ingratiation increases perceived intimacy but decreases perceived authenticity. Building on these perceptual responses, perceived intimacy and perceived authenticity jointly transmit the effects of AI ingratiation to user satisfaction and content iteration intention, indicating significant indirect effects through these dual mediating pathways. We further examine the moderating role of AI literacy and find that users with higher self-reported AI usage literacy are more responsive to AI ingratiation. Specifically, higher AI literacy strengthens the positive effect of AI ingratiation on perceived intimacy, which in turn enhances user satisfaction. Finally, a multi-group analysis reveals significant differences between advertising and academic contexts, suggesting that the effects of AI ingratiation vary across content generation scenarios. These findings highlight the dual-pathway and context-dependent nature of AI ingratiation in human–AI interaction.

item.title: Not All GenAI Disclosures Are Alike: How the Stage of GenAI Involvement Shapes Purchase Intention for Digital Games
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in digital game development, and disclosures on digital platforms make such use more visible to players. Prior research offers conflicting predictions regarding how users respond to such disclosure. Research on AI-generated products suggests that disclosure can reduce valuation because it weakens source-related beliefs tied to human creation. Research on games as interactive hedonic systems, however, suggests that players also evaluate games in terms of the experience they expect during play. Building on these perspectives, this study conceptualizes GenAI disclosure as the focal independent variable and proposes two pathways through which disclosure influences players’ purchase intention. First, GenAI disclosure decreases perceived effort, which lowers purchase intention. Second, GenAI disclosure can increase perceived novelty, which raises purchase intention, but this positive pathway depends on the stage of GenAI involvement described by the disclosure. Specifically, this positive effect is stronger under during-interaction involvement than under pre-interaction involvement. We test the model using a scenario-based online experiment in the context of digital games. The results show that GenAI disclosure reduces perceived effort relative to no disclosure, while its positive effect on perceived novelty emerges primarily when GenAI is described as contributing during gameplay rather than before gameplay. Willingness to pay is included as a supplementary outcome and shows directionally similar but weaker patterns. This study extends GenAI disclosure research to digital games and shows that the effect of disclosure depends not only on whether GenAI use is disclosed, but also on the stage of involvement described by that disclosure.

item.title: The Impacts of AI Recommendation Systems on User Loyalty in E-Commerce Platforms: Evidence from Gen Z Consumers in Ho Chi Minh City
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
This study examines the effects of the AI Recommendation System (ARS) on users’ loyalty on e-commerce platforms in Ho Chi Minh City. Integrating the S-O-R framework and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the study evaluates how characteristics of ARS, including personalization, accuracy, and transparency, affect trust and satisfaction. Data from 400 Gen Z consumers were analyzed using the Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results showed ARS significantly boosted trust and satisfaction, serving as key intermediates for long-term loyalty. This finding offers practical implications for businesses to optimize AI strategy and build sustainable customer relationships in the digital era.

item.title: Unpacking the Experience Economy of Role-Playing Conversational AI: A Grounded Theory Analysis
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
The rapid rise of role-playing conversational artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed human-AI interaction from task-oriented exchanges into immersive, scenario-based digital experiences. However, while prior studies predominantly evaluate AI through utilitarian performance or relational support, the holistic experiential structure of these novel interactions remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, this paper draws on the experience economy (4Es) framework to investigate how users experience role-playing conversational AI through the realms of entertainment, education, esthetics, and escapism. Using a grounded theory approach, this study analyzes 6,171 user comments from the Reddit community r/CharacterAI. Findings reveal that user-AI role-playing is fundamentally multidimensional: entertainment and escapism emerge as particularly salient, while educational and esthetic experiences are also clearly present. Ultimately, this study extends the 4Es framework into the context of generative AI, offering a foundational empirical understanding of this emerging form of experiential consumption.

item.title: A Large Language Model-Based Implementation of the Proposition-to-Requirement Mapping Framework for ESG Greenwashing Detection
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
This study implements and empirically evaluates the proposition-to-requirement mapping approach proposed in Wu, Li, & Cui (2026). Greenwashing detection in ESG reporting remains difficult because disclosures are narrative, heterogeneous, and often lack transparent evaluation criteria. This study proposes a proposition-level, framework-aligned method for analyzing ESG reports under the HKEX ESG Reporting Guide. The framework converts reports into structured text, decomposes them into atomic propositions, classifies propositions as disclosure, explanation, or residual, and semantically matches them to 192 binary disclosure requirements. Using Tencent’s ESG reports from 2022 to 2024 as a case, the results show that the proposed indicators are directionally consistent with changes in MSCI ESG ratings. The study provides an interpretable and traceable approach to ESG disclosure assessment.

item.title: Trust in AI-Assisted Newsvendor Decisions: Effects of Information Design
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
As artificial-intelligence-assisted tools become prevalent in supply chain inventory management, algorithmic trust critically determines the success of human-AI interaction. Based on the newsvendor decision making, this study primarily considers two key factors—information construal level and presentation format—to investigate how they affect trust in AI recommendation, alongside the moderating role of decision-makers' individual traits. Through an incentivized 2×3 between-subjects experiment, we empirically analyze the level of trust in AI decision-making tools, measured by participants' Mean Absolute Percentage Deviation (MAPD) from the AI-advised values across different groups. Results indicate that text-and-graphic and scenario-based presentation formats significantly reduce decision deviation and enhance AI trust, whereas the construal level shows no significant impact. Furthermore, while decision-making style significantly influences AI tool utilization frequency, it does not affect the actual adoption of AI advice. This study clarifies the mechanisms driving algorithmic trust in newsvendor settings and provides empirical evidence and guidelines for enterprises to optimize the front-end interactive design of AI decision assistants and implement differentiated promotion and literacy training strategies tailored to varying employee traits.

item.title: Mapping GenAI-Enabled Technical Features to Player Needs in Digital Games: A Needs-(Dis)Affordances-Features Framework
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly embedded in digital products, understanding how users experience GenAI-enabled products has become an important research issue. Prior research on GenAI products has mainly examined relatively static AI-generated outputs, with particular attention to disclosure, algorithmic source, authenticity, and perceived value. However, this literature offers limited insight into digital games, where GenAI may be incorporated not only into pre-generated components such as assets, text, and audio, but also into runtime systems such as adaptive dialogue, characters, and gameplay content. To address this gap, this study develops a Needs-(Dis)Affordances-Features framework for understanding how GenAI-enabled technical features shape players’ psychological need satisfaction and frustration in digital games. Drawing on the needs-affordances-features perspective, disaffordance, and self-determination theory, we conduct a grounded theory analysis of 3,096 reviews from 810 digital games on Steam identified through platform statements indicating GenAI involvement. The findings suggest that player responses are shaped less by AI-related labels or source cues than by the specific technical features through which GenAI is incorporated into the game. GenAI-enabled features such as generated assets, dialogue, and adaptive systems give rise to affordances and disaffordances that support or frustrate autonomy, competence, and relatedness. This study extends research on GenAI products to digital games by showing how feature-level GenAI integration, rather than AI origin alone, shapes player experience.

item.title: The Right Amount of “Human Touch”: The Curvilinear Effect of Embodied AI Agent Anthropomorphism on Consumer Usage Intention under Social Intrusiveness
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Anthropomorphic design in embodied AI agents often evokes ambivalent consumer responses, yet it remains a key strategy for enhancing users’ intention to use such agents. Based on three video-based scenario experiments with 438 participants, this study examines how anthropomorphism shapes consumers’ usage intentions. The results confirm an inverted-U-shaped relationship between anthropomorphism of embodied AI agents and usage intention. Further analyses reveal that likability and eeriness jointly mediate this curvilinear relationship: anthropomorphism exerts an inverted U-shaped effect on likability, which in turn positively influences usage intention, whereas anthropomorphism exerts a U-shaped effect on eeriness, which negatively influences usage intention. In addition, social intrusiveness functions as a boundary condition by (1) strengthening the curvilinear relationships between anthropomorphism and both likability and eeriness, and (2) moderating the indirect effects of likability and eeriness. These findings provide empirical support for applying social information processing theory to human–AI interaction and extend uncanny valley theory from emotional responses to usage intention. The study also offers practical implications for deploying embodied AI agents in customer service contexts.

item.title: AI Adoption and Firm Value: A Comparative Study of Chinese FinTech Companies
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Conventional approaches fail to capture how AI creates value in FinTech. This study develops a multidimensional AI adoption index and examines its relationship with firm value through comparative analysis of Tonghuashun, East Money Information, and Wind Information. Building on a comparative case analysis of three leading FinTech firms, complemented by panel data regression on firm–quarter observations (2018–2024), we find a U–shaped relationship–value emerges only after a threshold of AI integration is reached. Tonghuashun, the highest adopter, achieved 180% market capitalization growth since 2020, reaching RMB 169.94 billion, with monthly active users double its closest competitor. The findings indicate that strategic AI depth drives superior valuation, offering a replicable framework for evaluating AI value creation in emerging markets and extends the application of corporate valuation models to incorporate AI adoption as a measurable driver of firm value.

item.title: Theoretical Mechanisms and Framework of Perceived Algorithmic Bias Affecting Human-AI Collaborative Decision-Making Performance
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
Perceived algorithmic bias is defined as users' comprehensive subjective cognitive judgment, grounded in a cognitive attribution perspective, regarding whether an algorithmic system engages in differential treatment, whether its outcomes exhibit systematic deviations, and whether such differential treatment is justified. This study develops a theoretical model of perceived algorithmic bias and systematically elucidates the construct through three dimensions: perceived differential treatment, perceived outcome skew, and perceived lack of justification. The paper examines the mechanisms through which perceived algorithmic bias influences human-AI collaborative decision-making performance across three levels: cognitive processing, affect and morality, and human-AI interaction. It also analyzes the moderating roles of individual characteristics, algorithmic characteristics, and task characteristics. By systematically reviewing the conceptualizations of algorithmic bias and perceived algorithmic bias and clarifying their effects on and theoretical mechanisms underlying human-AI collaborative decision-making performance, this study offers theoretical implications for advancing research on perceived algorithmic bias. Future research may further develop a measurement scale for perceived algorithmic bias, enrich empirical investigations, test its underlying mechanisms, and explore its impact on human-AI collaborative decision-making performance across diverse application contexts.

item.title: How “AI Info” Labels Influence Social Media Posting Behavior? Evidence from Instagram
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
AI-generated content (AIGC) has reshaped content creation on social media, prompting platforms to adopt “AI Info” labels as transparency mechanisms. Drawing on signaling theory, this study examines how such labels influence content creators’ posting frequency. Using a propensity score matched difference-in-differences (PSM-DiD) design applied to a panel dataset of 237 Instagram creators observed from January 2023 to December 2025, we find that mandatory AI labeling significantly reduces creators’ weekly posting frequency. This study contributes to AI transparency research by demonstrating unintended behavioral consequences of disclosure policies for content creators, and offers implications for platform governance design.

item.title: Anthropomorphism and Relational Ontology of Purchase Intention in Generative AI Use: Insights from Mind Perception Theory and the Computers as Social Actors Paradigm
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
A human-centric understanding of purchase intention in generative AI contexts requires attention to how users interpret and experience AI systems under conditions of algorithmic opacity. Rather than treating AI adoption as the outcome of attribute evaluation, we argue that anthropomorphic cues shape how users construe the system itself. When AI is experienced as socially responsive rather than purely instrumental, evaluative emphasis shifts toward trust beliefs and interactional arousal. Drawing on Computers as Social Actors (CASA) and Mind Perception Theory, we theorize that anthropomorphism restructures the experiential architecture through which intention is formed. Using structural equation modeling with data from 526 generative AI users, results show that anthropomorphism influences purchase intention both directly and indirectly through trust and arousal, with relational mechanisms exerting stronger effects. By foregrounding user construal and experiential engagement, this research advances a human-centric framework for understanding AI adoption in opaque, interactive environments.

item.title: The Impact of AI-Generated Content on Brand Image: A Dual Perspective of Algorithm Appreciation and Aversion
item.description:
Journal of the Association for Information Systems
With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence technologies such as ChatGPT, Midjourney, and DALL-E, brands are increasingly leveraging AI to create marketing content. However, systematic research on how AI-generated content affects brand image remains scarce in academia, creating a critical knowledge gap for marketing practitioners. This study addresses this gap by investigating consumer attitudes toward brand use of AI-generated content and the underlying psychological mechanisms. Grounded in Algorithm Aversion theory and AI Technological Image Transfer theory, we examine whether brands should disclose AI involvement in their marketing content and how different AI participation approaches influence brand perception through three experimental studies (N=940). Results show that 100% AI-generated content significantly enhances brand image across all dimensions, with innovativeness showing the largest improvement. AI involvement approach significantly affects brand perception, with 100% AI producing the strongest effect. AI social identity emerges as the key psychological driver, while AI aversion paradoxically benefits 100% AI strategies through an “honesty effect.” This research challenges traditional algorithm aversion assumptions and provides guidance for brand AI marketing strategies.

item.title: Authenticity across human and synthetic influencers: a configurational review of source evaluation and social influence
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Authenticity has become a central concern in social media influencer research, yet its construction is examined differently across human, virtual, and artificial intelligence (AI)-mediated sources. This study examines how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across these influencer contexts. Methods This study conducted a corpus-based review of 1,676 English-language research articles indexed in the Web of Science Core Collection and Scopus between July 2017 and March 2026. BERTopic modeling was employed to identify recurring semantic topics, followed by an abductive, theory-informed synthesis organized around source ontology and the dominant basis of authenticity construction. Temporal changes in relative topic prevalence were examined across the eight complete calendar years from 2018 to 2025. Results The synthesis identified four configurations: relational human authenticity, curated human authenticity, humanized synthetic authenticity, and governed synthetic authenticity. Human-influencer research emphasizes biography, accumulated interaction, commercial congruence, and motive transparency, whereas synthetic-influencer research places greater weight on persona coherence, humanization, identity disclosure, ownership, automation, and accountability. Credibility, trust, parasocial interaction, social presence, and engagement emerge as closely associated evaluative processes. Temporal analysis revealed selective changes in relative topic prevalence, particularly concerning virtual-influencer credibility, humanization, and tourism-related applications, while most topics showed no clear linear trend. Discussion The findings provide a corpus- and method-dependent framework for understanding how authenticity is constructed and evaluated across human and synthetic influencer contexts. The framework highlights distinct evidential foundations underlying authenticity judgments and offers a basis for further research on source evaluation and social influence.

item.title: Feeling or thinking? User aversion to AI customer service in online education
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction AI customer service is increasingly integrated into online education, yet users may not always respond favorably to AI-assisted service interactions. Drawing on robotic role theory, this study examines how thinking and feeling AI customer service influence user aversion in online educational service encounters. Methods Three experiments were conducted to examine the effect of AI customer service type on user aversion (Study 1, N = 120), the mediating role of perceived intelligence (Study 2, N = 120), and the moderating role of AI identity disclosure timing (Study 3, N = 120). Across the three between-subjects experiments, thinking AI was operationalized through analytical, information-processing, and task-oriented communication, whereas feeling AI emphasized emotional recognition and relational support. Results The results show that feeling AI generates greater user aversion than thinking AI. Perceived intelligence mediated this effect, such that feeling AI is perceived as less intelligent, which in turn increases user aversion. Further, AI identity disclosure timing moderates the indirect effect through perceived intelligence. Early disclosure of AI identity attenuates the negative effect of feeling AI. Discussion These findings demonstrate that the effectiveness of different AI customer service types depends on the service context and highlight the importance of aligning AI communication with users’ task-oriented service needs.

item.title: From digital interaction to social connection: AI virtual humans as interactive learning partners for older adults
item.description:
Interactive Learning Environments
As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in educational and social interaction systems, its potential to alleviate digital exclusion and digital loneliness among older adults has attracted growing attention. Across two independent experiments, this study examined the association between AI-assisted interaction and digital loneliness among older adults, as well as the underlying psychological mechanisms. In Experiment 1, 90 older adults participated in a four-week randomized longitudinal experiment. A 2 (group) × 5 (time) mixed-design repeated-measures analysis of variance was conducted to compare changes in digital loneliness between an AI-assisted interaction group and a conventional interaction control group. The results showed that participants in the AI-assisted interaction group exhibited a more pronounced reduction in digital loneliness over the intervention period. Experiment 2 involved an independent sample of 210 participants and used PROCESS analyses to examine further the roles of perceived social support, evaluative emotional fulfillment, and technology acceptance. After controlling for baseline digital loneliness, perceived social support constituted a significant indirect pathway linking AI-assisted interaction to post-intervention digital loneliness, whereas the indirect effect through evaluative emotional fulfillment did not reach statistical significance. Technology acceptance further moderated the association between AI-assisted interaction and perceived social support. Taken together, these findings suggest that the association between AI-assisted interaction and reduced digital loneliness among older adults is primarily related to the perceived social support pathway. In contrast, evidence supporting the mediating role of evaluative emotional fulfillment remains insufficient. This study provides empirical evidence for understanding older adults’ experiences of social connectedness in inclusive AI-enabled environments. It underscores the importance of enhancing both the acceptability of AI-mediated interaction and its capacity to provide social support within educational and digital learning ecosystems.

item.title: Measuring Successful Cooperation in Human-AI Teamwork: Development and Validation of the Perceived Cooperativity and Teaming Perception Scales
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
As human–AI cooperation becomes increasingly prevalent, reliable instruments for assessing the subjective quality of cooperative human–AI interaction are needed. We introduce two theoretically grounded scales: the Perceived Cooperativity Scale (PCS), grounded in joint activity theory, and the Teaming Perception Scale (TPS), grounded in evolutionary cooperation theory. The PCS captures an agent’s perceived cooperative capability and practice within a single interaction sequence; the TPS captures the emergent sense of teaming arising from mutual contribution and support. Both scales were adapted for human–human cooperation to enable cross-agent comparisons. Across three studies (complete N=409) encompassing a cooperative card game (N1=94), LLM interaction (N2=182), and a decision-support system (N3=133), analyses of dimensionality, reliability, and validity indicated that both scales successfully differentiated between cooperation partners of varying cooperative quality and showed construct validity in line with expectations. The scales provide a basis for empirical investigation and system evaluation across a wide range of human–AI cooperation contexts.

item.title: Social robots in the real world: an analysis of social robot use based on consumer reviews
item.description:
Behaviour and Information Technology
Social robots (SR) are increasingly developed to support users’ mental health needs. Previous research suggests that potential benefits of interacting with SR include reduction in depressive symptoms, loneliness and improved quality of life. Despite the promising impact of short-term robot use, little is known about how SRs are used beyond short interaction in the research environment, and what spontaneous robot adoption looks like. Thus, in this study we set out to address this gap through an analysis of user-generated robot reviews. We analysed online reviews of commercially available SRs to characterise their impact and user experience. We used qualitative content analysis to extract salient themes from 1350 user-generated reviews, supplemented by sentiment analysis of the full sample of 9333 reviews. The content analysis revealed a list of SR use cases, user circumstances and characteristics, the impact of using the robots and ethical challenges experienced by users. The results suggest that self-reported benefits, such as improved mood, reduced depression and loneliness, are maintained through long-term robot use. This study provides a novel qualitative insight into user experiences and SR use in the real world that will inform future robotic development and implementation efforts.

item.title: Beyond accuracy: How humans evaluate legally correct but socially controversial legal advice from machines.
item.description:
Technology Mind and Behavior
AI systems are increasingly used to provide legal advice, raising questions about whether laypeople accept guidance from algorithms-especially when that advice is legally correct but socially controversial.We report a preregistered survey experiment with 3,348 adults in mainland China examining how people evaluate identical legal advice when it is attributed either to an AI system or to a human lawyer and when it is accompanied by reasoning or not.Contrary to expectations of algorithm aversion, attribution to an AI system has no net effect on perceived reasonableness.However, mediation analyses reveal opposing psychological pathways underlying this null result.AI-attributed advice is perceived as more objective, which increases perceived reasonableness, but also as less comprehensive and less attentive to special circumstances, which decreases perceived reasonableness.By contrast, providing legal reasoning substantially increases perceived reasonableness regardless of source, largely by enhancing perceptions of objectivity.Qualitative responses corroborate this tension between objectivity and contextual sensitivity in evaluations of legal advice.Together, these findings suggest that public responses to AI legal advisors are shaped not by rigid attitudes toward automation but by the balancing of competing normative expectations.The results have implications for theories of algorithm aversion and the design of AI recommendation systems in normatively salient domains.

item.title: Cognitive transparency and trust calibration in explainable AI systems: a psychological model of human-AI decision reliance
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is widely expected to improve transparency and support appropriate human reliance on AI-assisted decision-making. However, the psychological processes through which explainability relates to reliance remain insufficiently understood, and explainability, transparency, and trust have largely been examined separately. Objectives This study develops and tests a psychological model of cognitive transparency in which AI explainability, algorithmic transparency, and perceived AI accuracy are associated with human reliance on AI through cognitive understanding, cognitive trust, and trust calibration, with AI literacy as a boundary condition. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 342 AI users in South Korea in May and June 2026. Each participant evaluated one self-selected AI system that they had personally used; all constructs were measured by self-report. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. Results AI explainability (β = 0.349) and algorithmic transparency (β = 0.297) were positively associated with cognitive understanding. Cognitive understanding (β = 0.388) and, more strongly, perceived AI accuracy (β = 0.492) were associated with cognitive trust. Cognitive trust was associated with trust calibration (β = 0.631), which was associated with human reliance on AI (β = 0.600). All hypothesized indirect effects were significant, and AI literacy strengthened the association between AI explainability and cognitive understanding (β = 0.192). The model explained 36%–54% of the variance in the endogenous constructs and showed medium predictive power. Conclusion The findings are consistent with a sequence in which explainable AI relates to reliance through users’ understanding and trust judgments. Because all constructs were self-reported and measured at a single point in time, the results describe associations among users’ perceptions rather than causal effects, independently verified calibration, or objectively appropriate reliance. The findings suggest that AI developers in domains such as healthcare, education, and finance, where calibrated reliance is critical, should pair user-facing explanations with information about system accuracy and with AI literacy support.

item.title: Algorithm or Assembly? An Experimental Study of Recommendations by AI Versus Deliberative Mini-Publics in Democratic Decision-Making
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) renewed debates about who—or what—can legitimately contribute to democratic processes. While both AI and deliberative mini-publics can supplement citizens’ efforts to form judgments about issues, little is known about how citizens evaluate policy advice from these sources. In an online survey experiment with U.S. adults (N = 502), participants read a mock news story reporting a policy recommendation, attributed either to an AI system or a deliberative citizens’ assembly. Opinion climate was orthogonally varied to assess contextual influences. Results were split: citizens’ assemblies were rated fairer and more satisfying, but AI was perceived to be more useful. Opinion climate cues had no moderating effects. Further analysis indicated that acceptance of AI versus citizens’ assembly recommendations depends on individual factors, such as prior attitudes toward the issue and trust in AI. Findings offer theoretical and practical implications for designing democratic decision support systems.

item.title: Why this AI app? The impact of generative artificial intelligence on educators’ choices in educational apps
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior
In elementary education, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is being incorporated into educational applications, despite still-emerging evidence of its effects on children’s learning and development. Educators, who are already overwhelmed with choice in the commercial app space, may increasincly have to decide whether to incorporate GenAI-enabled apps for their classrooms. Thus, the present study investigates how mentioning GenAI in app store descriptions impacts K-6 educators’ selection of educational apps. Over two studies, K-6 educators (each n = 101) from Canada, the US, and the UK viewed and evaluated eight researcher-created educational math apps with and without GenAI. Study 1 tested whether mentioning GenAI in app descriptions affected educators’ app evaluations but found no effect. In Study 2, results from a repeated measures MANOVA revealed that educators rated apps without AI higher than those mentioning GenAI, but there were no significant effects of GenAI on likelihood to download or willingness to pay for apps. A hierarchical cluster analysis identified three distinct groups of educators: 1) selectors (n = 28), who exhibited a preference for downloading, rating, and paying for apps including GenAI; 2) agnostics (n = 59), who exhibit minimal preferences; and 3) avoiders (n = 14), who prefer apps without AI. Most educators were agnostic to the use of GenAI in educational apps, highlighting the need to support educators’ informed decisions about when to adopt GenAI tools and encourage critical evaluation of GenAI’s role in education. More research is needed to understand how educators’ GenAI preferences relate to their attitudes, knowledge, and use of GenAI.

item.title: Empathetic responses by AI legal assistants and user over-disclosure: evidence from an online survey experiment
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Introduction Generative AI legal assistants rely on users to describe events, evidence, and transaction histories, yet the same accounts may contain private information that is unnecessary for legal guidance. Empathetic language may affect how selectively users decide what to provide. Methods A one-factor between-subjects online survey experiment on Wenjuanxing randomly assigned 360 participants to rational, mildly empathetic, or highly empathetic AI legal responses (n = 120 per condition). Participants completed 1-5 Likert-type measures of parasocial response, privacy boundary judgment, and over-disclosure intention, together with related relational measures, and then answered an open-ended disclosure task. Results The empathy manipulation was successful, F (2,357) = 524.170, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.746. Stronger empathetic responses increased parasocial response (η 2 = 0.428), reduced privacy boundary judgment (η 2 = 0.242), and increased over-disclosure intention (η 2 = 0.406). The coded non-essential disclosure score rose from 0.994 in the rational condition to 6.132 in the highly empathetic condition, F (2,357) = 170.795, p < 0.001, and η 2 = 0.489. Necessary case facts remained stable, F (2,357) = 0.245, p = 0.783. Bootstrap analysis yielded an indirect effect through parasocial response of 0.214, 95% CI [0.151, 0.283], and a sequential indirect effect through parasocial response and privacy boundary judgment of 0.063, 95% CI [0.033, 0.098]. Discussion Within this consumer-dispute scenario, stronger empathetic cues reduced users' selectivity about which information was appropriate to provide. Data-minimization prompts and evidence-oriented questioning may help retain limited emotional support without encouraging unnecessary disclosure.

item.title: When loneliness amplifies the risk of problematic emotional dependence: perceived anthropomorphism and basic psychological need satisfaction in AI companion use
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Companion-oriented conversational AI can be experienced as socially responsive, yet evidence about problematic reliance requires construct clarity and noncausal interpretation. This study examined whether perceived anthropomorphism was associated with problematic AI-companion dependence directly and indirectly through basic psychological need satisfaction. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was completed by 666 adults in China who reported using a listed AI companion or conversational AI product during the preceding month. The nonclinical outcome was operationalized with six indicators spanning impaired control, distress, continued use, perceived understanding, emotion-regulation reliance, and displacement of offline communication. Measurement evidence was examined using reliability estimates, one-factor confirmatory models, and HTMT. Standardized composite-score regressions used HC3 robust standard errors, and the indirect association was evaluated with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Perceived anthropomorphism was positively associated with need satisfaction ( β = 0.569, p < 0.001). In the outcome model, need satisfaction ( β = 0.317, p < 0.001) and perceived anthropomorphism ( β = 0.385, p < 0.001) were both positively associated with problematic dependence. The standardized indirect association was 0.180 (95% bootstrap CI [0.137, 0.229]); R 2 was 0.323 for need satisfaction and 0.389 for problematic dependence. Conclusion The pattern is consistent with a need-satisfaction account of companion-oriented AI use, but the cross-sectional design does not establish temporal ordering, substitution, or causality. Design and policy implications should therefore focus on transparency, user agency, and safeguards against escalating reliance rather than treating anthropomorphism itself as inherently harmful.

item.title: From Representation to Relational Mentorship: User Perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors in AI-Mediated Intangible Cultural Heritage Learning
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
This study presents a convergent mixed-methods empirical investigation of user perceptions of Virtual Heritage Mentors (VHMs) in AI-mediated intangible cultural heritage learning. The study draws on an online survey of 370 participants and semi-structured interviews with 20 independently recruited participants, all of whom were ethnically Chinese. The results indicated that participants prioritized interactive explanation, clarification, and guided support over visual realism. Trust was associated with cultural accuracy, contextual grounding, transparency, and respect for heritage communities. Emotional resonance was valued less as anthropomorphic simulation than as pedagogical care expressed through patience, encouragement, re-explanation, and responsiveness. Participants also envisioned VHMs as adaptive learning companions while emphasizing that AI should complement rather than replace human practitioners. These findings empirically support and refine the proposed VHM framework by highlighting relational mediation, relational mentorship, co-transmission, and human–AI complementarity as key design priorities. The study argues for shifting digital heritage design from representation alone toward relational, culturally accountable support for heritage learning and transmission.

item.title: Using AI, Doubting AI: Developer Mental Models and Trust in AI-Assisted Software Work
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Generative AI has entered software work with remarkable speed, yet trust in its output remains unsettled. This study examines how developers and learners navigate AI-assisted software work through mental models and trust. Analyzing 40,052 responses from the 2025 Stack Overflow Developer Survey, the findings reveal a durable paradox: professionals use AI more intensively than learners but trust it less, evaluating its capability for complex tasks more cautiously. The primary threat to trust is corrective labor, such as debugging time, rather than code legibility. Cluster analysis identifies four mental-model profiles—open but light users, skeptical dependents, resistant/disengaged respondents, and enthusiastic adopters—with professionals disproportionately concentrated in skeptical dependence. Ultimately, adoption does not settle the trust question; instead, mental models act as interpretive filters through which developers decide when to rely, verify, and pull back.
